notes.meaning: The groom announces that he has arrived in his garden to enjoy its sweet fruits, spices, wine, and milk. He then invites his companions to feast and drink freely. In the traditional reading, Christ gladly answers the call of his church, rejoicing in the obedience of his people and welcoming them to feast on his spiritual grace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see this as a celebration of physical intimacy on a wedding night, where the garden pictures the mutual delights of husband and wife.

notes.meaning: The woman rests in bed half-asleep, but her heart stirs when she hears her beloved knocking at the door. He addresses her with tender, loving names and asks to come in out of the wet night air. This portrays a believer who has grown spiritually sluggish, while Christ patiently knocks at the heart through his Word and Spirit to restore close fellowship.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars understand this opening scene as the beginning of a troubling dream about intimacy and emotional distance between married lovers.

notes.meaning: The woman makes excuses instead of getting up right away. She has already taken off her robe and washed her feet for the night, so getting out of bed feels inconvenient. This shows how easily people offer selfish, petty excuses to put off answering Christ when he calls them to rise and follow him.

The beloved reaches his hand through the door opening to unlatch the lock, and her heart is deeply stirred for him. When gentle words alone do not move her, his personal touch reaches her conscience. The soul is suddenly gripped with deep affection and sorrow for having kept him outside.

She finally rises from her bed to open the door for her beloved. As she touches the wooden bolt, sweet-smelling myrrh from his hands covers her own fingers. Even when Christ withdraws after being neglected, the sweet fragrance of his grace remains behind to soften the heart and spark true repentance.

She opens the door, but her beloved has already turned and walked away. Her heart sinks with grief as she runs into the night, calling out to him without receiving an answer. Christ sometimes hides his comforting presence for a season to teach believers not to take him for granted and to seek him more earnestly in prayer.

While searching the city in the dark, the night watchmen find her, strike her, and take away her veil. Instead of helping her find her beloved, the city guards mistreat and dishonor her. This pictures how harsh or unfaithful church leaders can wound the consciences of seeking souls instead of gently guiding them back to Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see this harsh beating by the watchmen as part of the woman's dream, reflecting her inner guilt and fear of losing her dignity.

notes.meaning: The woman turns to the young women of Jerusalem and begs them for help. She asks them to tell her beloved, if they find him, that she is faint and aching with love. Having lost the sense of his closeness, her soul can find no rest until their communion is restored.

The daughters of Jerusalem ask why her beloved is better than any other lover. They wonder what makes him so extraordinary that she is willing to suffer and plead so intensely for him. When others see a believer's deep devotion to Christ, it often sparks their own curiosity to learn who he truly is.

She answers by praising her beloved as radiant and ruddy, standing out above ten thousand others. He possesses unmatched health, vigor, and royal dignity. Traditionally, his brightness reflects his spotless, sinless life, while the ruddy red color points to his suffering and death on the cross.

She describes his head as purest gold and his hair as thick, wavy, and raven black. The gold symbolizes his royal crown, divine majesty, and supreme rule. His dark, thick hair represents his youthful strength and vigorous life, showing that Christ is an everlasting and glorious King.

His eyes are compared to doves resting beside flowing streams, washed in milk and set like precious stones. Doves convey a sense of gentleness, purity, and innocent love. This shows that Christ looks upon his people with eyes of tender mercy and deep sympathy rather than harsh condemnation.

His cheeks are compared to mounds of fragrant spices, and his lips to lilies dripping with sweet myrrh. His face radiates warmth, beauty, and comforting presence. His lips represent the words of grace and truth that flow from the Gospel, bringing refreshing peace to troubled hearts.

She describes his hands as golden rods set with beryl jewels, and his body like smooth ivory inlaid with blue sapphires. These royal images picture strength, preciousness, and noble craftsmanship. They point to the glorious power of Christ's works and the pure, unchanging beauty of his person.

His legs are like marble pillars standing on bases of fine gold, and his stature is as noble as the great cedars of Lebanon. Pillars represent firm and unshakeable strength. Christ stands solid and unchanging, bearing the full weight of his people's salvation with regal majesty.

She summarizes his beauty by declaring that his mouth is full of sweetness and that he is altogether lovely in every way. He is both her beloved and her companion. In the eyes of faith, Christ has no defect, serving not only as the glorious Lord of the church but also as a faithful and tender friend to all who trust him.
